sections.overview: Arenicola marina is a burrowing marine annelid in the lugworm family Arenicolidae. It is called the blow lug or lugworm in English and arénicole des pêcheurs in French.
sections.identification: Adults are usually 10–25 cm long; sources give no sex-specific range or standard body width, height or mass. The firm, cylindrical body has a blunt head without eyes or feelers, a middle region with branching red gills, and a narrow rear region without gills or bristles. Its color ranges from greenish yellow or dark green to red, pink and nearly black. It may be confused with the related black lug, Arenicola defodiens, which is generally larger and darker and leaves a neater, tighter cast; A. marina usually leaves a messy cast beside a separate feeding funnel.
sections.habitat: It occurs across much of the North Atlantic, from Arctic shores to the Mediterranean, including the North Sea and western European coasts. It lives in fine sand or muddy sand on tidal flats, sheltered beaches and estuaries, in a deep U- or J-shaped burrow.
sections.diet: The worm swallows sediment at the head end of its burrow and digests the organic particles, bacteria, microalgae and tiny animals among the grains. It rejects the cleaned mineral sand behind it as a coiled or tangled cast at the surface.
sections.behavior: Most of its life is spent hidden in its burrow; the funnel and cast at low tide reveal where it feeds and defecates, while periodic water flow ventilates its gill-bearing region.
sections.reproduction: The sexes are separate, and spawning is usually synchronized in early autumn, though timing can vary among local populations. Females retain eggs in their burrows while males release sperm onto the sediment; incoming seawater carries sperm into the galleries for fertilization.
sections.ecology: By turning over sediment and pumping oxygenated water through deep burrows, lugworms alter the conditions of tidal-flat habitats and increase oxygen exchange below the surface.
sections.conservation: It remains widespread but is collected as fishing bait; harvesting can disturb sediments and affect local populations, while the sources reviewed provide no global threat category.
